publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 7 On Sacred Scripture's sense and interpretation, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS 245–mid-276): sense as Scripture's letter agreeing with the Spirit's intent; against enthusiasm and multiplex sense in one utterance; interpretation defined; five hermeneutic norms; interpreter's regeneration and languages; Hebrew/Greek authentic texts; threefold medium; didactic vs judicial interpretation; against papal sole interpreter; six illegitimate measures of sense; public and private interpretive power. Cap. 8 On Scripture's efficacy begins mid PHYS 276; Cap. 6 complete; the rest of the Syntagma remains.

source_text: CAPUT SEPTIMUM. De sensu & interpretatione sacrae Scripturae. Haec de claritate: sequitur sensus, qui est sacrae Scripturae proprietas, qua illius litera cum Spiritus sancti intentione exactissime congruit. LITERA Scripturae sacrae est instar corporis sive signi externi & corporei, quo regnum Dei, quod est in potentia seu virtute, 1. Cor. 4.20. ad captum nostrum declaratur: sensus vero est veluti spiritus vitalis & anima, qua auctoris mens quasi in aprico ponitur & ad vivum exprimitur per demonstrationem spiritualem & efficacem, 1. Cor. 2.4. Extra quam litera Scriptura non est Dei, sed tua, perinde ut imago regis ex auro conflata non est regis, sed canis, si ipsissimum illud aurum igne solutum in imaginem canis distinguatur, ut alicubi contra haereticas interpretationes Irenaeus disserit. Procul autem hic habeatur Enthusiastus, qui Scripturam, literamque sacram, externumque verbum, quod docetur, prorsus adspernatur & ante illud speculationes & phantasmata sua habet non sine opinione singularis sanctimoniae: de quo beatus Lutherus in convivalibus titulo de fanaticis & sectis vaticinatus est, quemque doctissimus Philippus Marnixius solide refutavit.
english:
CHAPTER SEVEN
On Sacred Scripture's sense and interpretation
So far concerning clarity: next comes sense. Sense is Sacred Scripture's property by which its letter agrees most exactly with the Holy Spirit's intention.

Sacred Scripture's letter is like a body, or an outward bodily sign, by which God's kingdom — which is in power or virtue (1 Cor. 4:20) — is declared to our grasp. Sense is like the vital spirit and soul by which the author's mind is set, as it were, in the open and expressed to the life by a spiritual and effectual demonstration (1 Cor. 2:4). Apart from that sense the letter of Scripture is not God's, but yours — just as a king's image cast in gold is not the king's but a dog's, if that very gold is melted by fire and cast into a dog's image, as Irenaeus somewhere argues against heretical interpretations.

Here let the Enthusiast be kept far off — the one who utterly spurns Scripture, the sacred letter, and the outward word that is taught, and sets his own speculations and phantasms before it, not without an opinion of singular holiness. Blessed Luther prophesied of such in his Table Talk under the title on fanatics and sects, and the most learned Philip Marnix solidly refuted them.

source_text: Solidus vero cibus his quatuor potissimum continetur: 1. Prophetarum suarum ad sua definita tempora, loca, res & personas vera & certa accommodatione. 2. Umbrarum Leviticarum ad corpus & veritatem suam in N.T. exhibitam exacta & plena reductione. 3. Gubernationis divinae per universam Scripturam typice adumbratae ad veritatem suam convenienti applicatione. 4. Totius creatae universitatis, quae Creatoris sui imago est, & in qua totius sacrae Scripturae litera, parabolae & phrases obviae sunt, ad veritatem suam ibidem descriptam concinna & indubitata explicatione. XXXI. Est autem ea interpretandi, judicandique potestas duplex, vel publica vel privata. Utraque vocatione & dono singulari nititur. XXXII. Potestas privatim judicandi de sacrae Scripturae sensu in rebus ad salutem necessariis est omnium fidelium ad confirmationem fidei propriae & aedificationem alienam, secundum charitatis legem, doni accepti mensuram & vocationis diversam rationem. Hanc Theologi Leidenenses recte deducunt synopsi purioris Theologiae disp.5. thes.29. ex Joh. 10.3. Matth. 7.15. 1. Cor. 10.15. 1. Joh. 4.1. Hocque judicandi genus nititur dono discretionis, 1. Cor. 2.15. Heb. 5.14. Phil. 1.10. Potestas publice judicandi de veritate interpretationis est eorum duntaxat, qui peculiari vocatione & dono interpretandi ad hoc instructi sunt. Hujus vocationis gradus enumerantur Eph. 4.11. Donum vero indicatur Rom. 12.6. 1. Cor. 14.3.29. Et quanquam inter alios quoque Christianos omnibus seculis exstiterunt, qui per preces, assiduamque sacrae Scripturae lectionem & meditationem, donum sacras literas ad usus publicos interpretandi & spiritus probandi ampliori mensura, quam nonnulli pastores acceperint; tamen donum illud inter eos praecipue quaerendum est, quos Deus ad Ecclesiam suam publice docendam peculiariter vocavit, Malach. 2.6.7.
english: Solid food is contained chiefly in these four: (1) the true and certain accommodation of the prophets to their defined times, places, things, and persons; (2) the exact and full reduction of Levitical shadows to their body and truth exhibited in the New Testament; (3) the fitting application of the divine governance typified through all Scripture to its truth; (4) the neat and undoubted explanation of the whole created universe — which is its Creator's image, and in which the letter, parables, and phrases of all Sacred Scripture lie ready — to its truth described in the same place.

XXXI. The power of interpreting and judging is twofold: public or private. Both rest on vocation and a singular gift. XXXII. The power of privately judging Sacred Scripture's sense in things necessary to salvation belongs to all the faithful, for confirming their own faith and edifying others, according to the law of charity, the measure of the gift received, and the diverse reason of calling. The Leiden theologians rightly draw this from the Synopsis of Purer Theology (disp. 5, th. 29) out of John 10:3; Matt. 7:15; 1 Cor. 10:15; 1 John 4:1. This kind of judging rests on the gift of discernment (1 Cor. 2:15; Heb. 5:14; Phil. 1:10).

The power of publicly judging the truth of interpretation belongs only to those who by peculiar vocation and gift of interpreting are furnished for it. The grades of this vocation are listed in Eph. 4:11; the gift is indicated in Rom. 12:6; 1 Cor. 14:3, 29. And although in every age there have also been other Christians who by prayers and assiduous reading and meditation of Sacred Scripture received the gift of interpreting the sacred letters for public uses and of proving spirits in fuller measure than some pastors; yet that gift is chiefly to be sought among those whom God has peculiarly called to teach his Church publicly (Mal. 2:6–7).

source_text: XIX. Usus & applicatio rerum est, qua illae ad sensum & normam sanorum verborum ex intentione ac mente Spiritus signis fallibilibus expressa enarrantur, catholica dogmata proprie explicantur & confirmantur, heterodoxa & falsa solide ac nervose confutantur, mores corrupti emendantur, boni praecipiuntur, moesti ac pusillanimes eriguntur, securi & audaces terrentur, ut homo Dei perfectus & ad omne bonum opus instructus efficiatur. Fundamentum hujus interpretationis extat 2. Tim. 3.16. Rom. 15.4. Jud. 20-23. XX. Deinde interpretatio alia est didascalica, alia critica seu judicialis. Hanc distinctionem Bellarminus lib.3. de verbo Dei, cap.10. in responsione ad argumentum 16. admittit. XXI. Didascalica interpretatio est, quae fit tanquam a doctore idoneis rationibus perite adhibitis, secundum catholicas & manifestas interpretandi leges. XXII. Estque ordinaria aut extraordinaria. XXIII. Ordinaria est, quae nititur aequipollentia vel consequentia nullam habente controversiam, aut habente saltem testimonium consentiens & notorium ab Ecclesia primitiva.
english: XIX. The use and application of things is that by which they are related to the sense and norm of sound words expressed by fallible signs from the Spirit's intention and mind; catholic dogmas are properly explained and confirmed; heterodox and false things are solidly and vigorously confuted; corrupt manners are amended; good things are commanded; the sorrowful and faint-hearted are raised up; the secure and bold are terrorstruck — so that the man of God may be made perfect and furnished for every good work. The foundation of this interpretation stands in 2 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 15:4; Jude 20–23.

XX. Next, interpretation is either didactic or critical (judicial). Bellarmine admits this distinction (On the Word of God 3.10, reply to argument 16). XXI. Didactic interpretation is what is done as by a teacher, with fit reasons skillfully applied, according to the catholic and manifest laws of interpreting. XXII. It is either ordinary or extraordinary. XXIII. Ordinary is what rests on equivalence or consequence that has no controversy, or that at least has agreeing and notorious testimony from the primitive Church.

source_text: XI. Objectum est textus Biblicus tota secum serie cohaerens. Clemens Alexandrinus lib.7. Strom. textum appellat to soma tes tou Theou propheteias, corpus & telam prophetiae, in qua, tanquam subjecta materia, considerantur verba, in verbis significatus proprius aut tropicus, ex quibus sensus ita elicitur, ut interpres neque se a textu, neque a textu verba, neque a verbis sensum separari permittat. Aliud vero est sensus, aliud significatus. Ille dictorum integratorum est, hic verborum singulorum. Ille ex horum natura & ordine, quo se in dictis Scripturae respiciunt, elicitur, & a Spiritu sancto perficitur, cujus solius interpretatio vera est, sicut & in civilibus juris legumque constitutionibus earum interpretatio ad eum pertinet, qui eas constituit. Caeterum, textus Hebraicus V.T. notis Masoreticis instructus & correctus, prout a nobis Christianis in probatis, etiam Judaicis, exemplaribus asservatur, usurpatur: tum ratione dictionum & sententiarum, tum ratione elementorum, sive literae sint, sive puncta, ab omni corruptela ita est immunis, ut divina NORMA, canon ac regula sit, ad quam omnes omnino versiones linguarum caeterarum, & praesertim versio Latina vulgata, examinari & emendari debeat. Textus vero N.T. Graecus, in probatis codicibus asservatus, a corruptelis eodem in modum adeo est immunis, ut sit exactissima norma, ad quam omnes versiones & interpretationes examinari & corrigi debeant. Illud prolixe demonstrat D. Glassius lib.1. philol. sacrae tract.1 & 2.
english: XI. The object is the biblical text cohering with itself in its whole series. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 7) calls the text the body and fabric of God's prophecy, in which, as subject-matter, words are considered, and in the words a proper or tropical signification, from which the sense is so drawn that the interpreter permits neither himself to be severed from the text, nor words from the text, nor sense from the words. Sense is one thing, signification another. The former belongs to whole utterances; the latter to single words. Sense is drawn from the nature and order of the words as they regard one another in Scripture's sayings, and is perfected by the Holy Spirit alone — whose alone is true interpretation, just as in civil law the interpretation of statutes belongs to him who constituted them.

Further: the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, furnished and corrected with Masoretic notes as preserved by us Christians in approved copies (even Jewish ones), is so free from all corruption — whether of diction and sentences or of letters and points — that it is the divine NORM, canon, and rule by which all versions in other tongues, and especially the Latin Vulgate, ought to be examined and emended. The Greek text of the New Testament, preserved in approved codices, is likewise so free from corruptions that it is the most exact norm by which all versions and interpretations ought to be examined and corrected. Glassius demonstrates this at length in Sacred Philology, Book 1, tracts 1 and 2.

source_text: XXX. Caeterum ex iis, quae hactenus docuimus, recte inferimus, interpretationem sublestam esse neque satis solidam & legitimam, quae fit 1. Secundum sensum, qua ille in vulgata versione canonizatus est: quia impingit in legitimae interpretationis objectum. Nam haec versio, quia non est, non est authentica, ac ne textus quidem quem interpres primo debet interpretari. 2. Secundum sensum, qua ille a ratione veteris Adami dependet: quia sacrae Scripturae sensus supra hanc rationem est a Dei spiritu & cujus scriptoris voluntate mensuratur. 3. Secundum sensum, qua ille a sensu patrum mensuratur: quia ita negligeretur textus, qui sensum ex se parit; quia aut omnium patrum sensus erit regula aut quorundam duntaxat — at non hoc neque illud; quia Hermeneuticae legibus repugnat, quae patres agnoscunt quidem manuductores, non tamen infallibiles; quia saepicule genuinum Scripturae sensum haud assecuti sunt; quia non raro secuti sunt sensus erroneos. 4. Secundum sensum, qua a traditionibus non scriptis integratur. 5. Secundum sensum, qua ab Ecclesia aut a Papa determinatus est, ob rationes easdem quas ad aph. 26. protulimus. 6. Sine discrimine infantilis & virilis aetatis, lactis & solidi cibi, quod in docendo prudenter observat Apostolus, 1. Cor. 3.1.2. Heb. 5.12-14.
english: XXX. From what we have taught so far we rightly infer that an interpretation is weak and not solid enough or legitimate which is made (1) according to the sense as canonized in the Vulgate version — because it strikes against the object of legitimate interpretation: that version is not authentic, nor even the text the interpreter ought first to interpret; (2) according to the sense as it depends on old Adam's reason — because Sacred Scripture's sense stands above that reason and is measured by God's Spirit and the will of its writer; (3) according to the sense as measured by the fathers' sense — because then the text that bears sense from itself would be neglected; because either all the fathers' sense or only some would be the rule — neither works; because it conflicts with hermeneutical laws that acknowledge the fathers as guides, not as infallible; because they often missed the genuine sense; because they not rarely followed erroneous senses; (4) according to the sense as completed by unwritten traditions; (5) according to the sense as determined by the Church or by the Pope, for the same reasons we gave at Aph. 26; (6) without distinguishing childish and mature age, milk and solid food, which the Apostle wisely observes in teaching (1 Cor. 3:1–2; Heb. 5:12–14).
